## Proposition 13.18
**Statement:** To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.

**Step 1.** Let the diameter of the given sphere be AB, and set AB so that it is a given rational straight line. We shall set out the side of each of the five regular solid figures inscribed in this sphere and compare them with one another.

**Step 2.** [Side of the Pyramid (Tetrahedron)] By 13.13, the square on the diameter AB of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the inscribed pyramid. That is, sq(AB) = (3/2) sq(s_pyramid). Therefore sq(s_pyramid) = (2/3) sq(AB). Cut AB at C so that AC = 2 CB (by 6.10, cutting a line in a given ratio). Then AC = (2/3)AB and CB = (1/3)AB. By 2.4 and the proportions, sq(AB) : sq(s_pyramid) = 3 : 2. Therefore sq(s_pyramid) = (2/3) sq(AB). Since AB is rational, sq(AB) is rational, and (2/3) sq(AB) is a definite expressible area; the side of the pyramid is thus determinate.

**Step 3.** [Side of the Octahedron] By 13.14, the square on the diameter AB is double the square on the side of the inscribed octahedron. That is, sq(AB) = 2 sq(s_octa). Therefore sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB). Bisect AB at D (by 1.10). Then sq(AB) = 2 sq(AD) by the relationship of the diameter to its half, and the side of the octahedron is such that its square equals the square on AD together with itself, i.e., sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB).

**Step 4.** [Side of the Cube] By 13.15, the square on the diameter AB is triple the square on the side of the inscribed cube. That is, sq(AB) = 3 sq(s_cube). Therefore sq(s_cube) = (1/3) sq(AB). The side of the cube is thus also determinate.

**Step 5.** [Comparison: Pyramid side vs. Octahedron side vs. Cube side] We now have: sq(s_pyramid) = (2/3) sq(AB), sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB), and sq(s_cube) = (1/3) sq(AB). Since (2/3) > (1/2) > (1/3), and all are squares on positive lengths applied to the same sq(AB), it follows that sq(s_pyramid) > sq(s_octa) > sq(s_cube). Since greater squares correspond to greater sides (for positive magnitudes), we have s_pyramid > s_octa > s_cube, by 5.8 and the ordering of the ratios.

**Step 6.** [More precise comparison of Pyramid and Octahedron sides] Now sq(s_pyramid) = (2/3) sq(AB) and sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB). So sq(s_pyramid) : sq(s_octa) = (2/3) : (1/2) = 4 : 3. That is, the square on the side of the pyramid is to the square on the side of the octahedron as 4 is to 3. By 5.14 (composition), and since 4 = 3 + 1, the excess of sq(s_pyramid) over sq(s_octa) has the ratio 1 : 3 to sq(s_octa). Hence sq(s_pyramid) is four-thirds of sq(s_octa).

**Step 7.** [More precise comparison of Octahedron and Cube sides] Similarly, sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB) and sq(s_cube) = (1/3) sq(AB). So sq(s_octa) : sq(s_cube) = (1/2) : (1/3) = 3 : 2. That is, the square on the side of the octahedron is to the square on the side of the cube as 3 is to 2. Hence sq(s_octa) is three-halves of sq(s_cube). Also, since sq(AB) = 2 sq(s_octa) and sq(AB) = 3 sq(s_cube), we have 2 sq(s_octa) = 3 sq(s_cube).

**Step 8.** [Summary of rational comparisons] Therefore: sq(s_pyramid) : sq(s_octa) : sq(s_cube) = 4 : 3 : 2, since sq(s_pyramid) = (2/3) sq(AB), sq(s_octa) = (1/2) sq(AB), sq(s_cube) = (1/3) sq(AB), and multiplying each by 6/sq(AB) gives 4, 3, 2 respectively. These three sides are commensurable in square with one another by D10.1.1 and D10.1.2, since their squares have ratios expressible as ratios of numbers.

**Step 9.** [Side of the Icosahedron] By 13.16, the side of the icosahedron inscribed in the given sphere is the irrational straight line called minor. Therefore the side of the icosahedron is not commensurable with AB, and it is specifically a minor line.

**Step 10.** [Side of the Dodecahedron] By 13.17, the side of the dodecahedron inscribed in the given sphere is the irrational straight line called apotome. Therefore the side of the dodecahedron is not commensurable with AB, and it is specifically an apotome.

**Step 11.** [The icosahedron side is not equal to the dodecahedron side] Since the side of the icosahedron is a minor irrational and the side of the dodecahedron is an apotome, and a minor and an apotome are distinct kinds of irrational lines (a minor being the difference of two lines incommensurable in square whose squares sum to a rational area with a medial rectangle, and an apotome being the difference of two lines commensurable in square only with the greater commensurable with a rational line), these two sides are not equal to one another, for by 10.111, an apotome is not the same as a minor. Furthermore, they are each incommensurable with the sides of the pyramid, octahedron, and cube, since those three sides are rational in square relative to the diameter.

**Step 12.** [Comparison of icosahedron and dodecahedron sides] Consider the icosahedron. In the construction of 13.16, the side of the icosahedron inscribed in a sphere of diameter AB involves the side of the decagon and side of the hexagon inscribed in a certain circle. By 13.10, the square on the side of the pentagon inscribed in a circle equals the sum of the squares on the sides of the hexagon and decagon inscribed in the same circle. By 13.9, when the side of the hexagon and side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle are added, the resulting line is cut in extreme and mean ratio, with the hexagon side as the greater segment. Since the dodecahedron's side, by the construction of 13.17, is related to the side of the pentagon face inscribed in certain circles of the dodecahedron, the comparison ultimately depends on the relative constructions within the same sphere.

**Step 13.** [Conclusion] We have therefore set out the sides of all five regular solid figures inscribed in the same sphere. The side of the pyramid is the greatest, the side of the cube is the least among the three rational (in square) sides, and the side of the octahedron is between them, with their squares in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2. The side of the icosahedron is a minor irrational line, and the side of the dodecahedron is an apotome; these two are each irrational and of distinct species, and neither is commensurable with the other three sides. This is what was required to be shown.

heath_proof_text: Let AB, the diameter of the given sphere, be set out, and let it be cut at C so that AC is equal to CB, and at D so that AD is double of DB; let the semicircle AEB be described on AB, from C, D let CE, DF be drawn at right angles to AB, and let AF, FB, EB be joined. Then, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. Convertendo, therefore, BA is one and a half times AD. But, as BA is to AD, so is the square on BA to the square on AF, [V. Def. 9, VI. 8] for the triangle AFB is equiangular with the triangle AFD; therefore the square on BA is one and a half times the square on AF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. [XIII. 13] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore AF is equal to the side of the pyramid. Again, since AD is double of DB, therefore AB is triple of BD. But, as AB is to BD, so is the square on AB to the square on BF; [VI. 8, V. Def. 9] therefore the square on AB is triple of the square on BF. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also triple of the square on the side of the cube. [XIII. 15] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore BF is the side of the cube. And, since AC is equal to CB, therefore AB is double of BC. But, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the square on BE; therefore the square on AB is double of the square on BE. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also double of the square on the side of the octahedron. [XIII. 14] And AB is the diameter of the given sphere; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron. Next, let AG be drawn from the point A at right angles to the straight line AB, let AG be made equal to AB, let GC be joined, and from H let HK be drawn perpendicular to AB. Then, since GA is double of AC, for GA is equal to AB, and, as GA is to AC, so is HK to KC, therefore HK is also double of KC. Therefore the square on HK is quadruple of the square on KC; therefore the squares on HK, KC, that is, the square on HC, is five times the square on KC. But HC is equal to CB; therefore the square on BC is five times the square on CK. And, since AB is double of CB, and, in them, AD is double of DB, therefore the remainder BD is double of the remainder DC. Therefore BC is triple of CD; therefore the square on BC is nine times the square on CD. But the square on BC is five times the square on CK; therefore the square on CK is greater than the square on CD; therefore CK is greater than CD. Let CL be made equal to CK, from L let LM be drawn at right angles to AB, and let MB be joined. Now, since the square on BC is five times the square on CK, and AB is double of BC, and KL double of CK, therefore the square on AB is five times the square on KL. But the square on the diameter of the sphere is also five times the square on the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. [XIII. 16] And AB is the diameter of the sphere; therefore KL is the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron has been described; therefore KL is a side of the hexagon in the said circle. [IV. 15] And, since the diameter of the sphere is made up of the side of the hexagon and two of the sides of the decagon inscribed in the same circle, [XIII. 16] and AB is the diameter of the sphere, while KL is a side of the hexagon, and AK is equal to LB, therefore each of the straight lines AK, LB is a side of the decagon inscribed in the circle from which the icosahedron has been described. And, since LB belongs to a decagon, and ML to a hexagon, for ML is equal to KL, since it is also equal to HK, being the same distance from the centre, and each of the straight lines HK, KL is double of KC, therefore MB belongs to a pentagon. [XIII. 10] But the side of the pentagon is the side of the icosahedron; [XIII. 16] therefore MB belongs to the icosahedron. Now, since FB is a side of the cube, let it be cut in extreme and mean ratio at N, and let NB be the greater segment; therefore NB is a side of the dodecahedron. [XIII. 17] And, since the square on the diameter of the sphere was proved to be one and a half times the square on the side AF of the pyramid, double of the square on the side BE of the octahedron and triple of the side FB of the cube, therefore, of parts of which the square on the diameter of the sphere contains six, the square on the side of the pyramid contains four, the square on the side of the octahedron three, and the square on the side of the cube two. Therefore the square on the side of the pyramid is fourthirds of the square on the side of the octahedron, and double of the square on the side of the cube; and the square on the side of the octahedron is one and a half times the square on the side of the cube. The said sides, therefore, of the three figures, I mean the pyramid, the octahedron and the cube, are to one another in rational ratios. But the remaining two, I mean the side of the icosahedron and the side of the dodecahedron, are not in rational ratios either to one another or to the aforesaid sides; for they are irrational, the one being minor [XIII. 16] and the other an apotome [XIII. 17]. That the side MB of the icosahedron is greater than the side NB of the dodecahedron we can prove thus. For, since the triangle FDB is equiangular with the triangle FAB, [VI. 8] proportionally, as DB is to BF, so is BF to BA. [VI. 4] And, since the three straight lines are proportional, as the first is to the third, so is the square on the first to the square on the second; [V. Def. 9, VI. 20] therefore, as DB is to BA, so is the square on DB to the square on BF; therefore, inversely, as AB is to BD, so is the square on FB to the square on BD. But AB is triple of BD; therefore the square on FB is triple of the square on BD. But the square on AD is also quadruple of the square on DB, for AD is double of DB; therefore the square on AD is greater than the square on FB; therefore AD is greater than FB; therefore AL is by far greater than FB. And, when AL is cut in extreme and mean ratio, KL is the greater segment, inasmuch as LK belongs to a hexagon, and KA to a decagon; [XIII. 9] and, when FB is cut in extreme and mean ratio, NB is the greater segment; therefore KL is greater than NB. But KL is equal to LM; therefore LM is greater than NB. Therefore MB, which is a side of the icosahedron, is by far greater than NB which is a side of the dodecahedron.
